title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours: Release date, OLED, specs and latest leaks
content:
Macworld





The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, the rumours are becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss.
Multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way. If they’re accurate, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro will arrive as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display, next-generation Apple silicon, and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout.
The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the rumoured budget-friendly MacBook Neo.
There are still questions over pricing. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures are expected to make the new models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro. Apple is also expected to keep touchscreen technology exclusive to its premium laptops initially, with no indication that it will come to the MacBook Air or MacBook Neo in the first generation. Read on for a complete roundup of the latest touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours, including what the most reliable sources are saying, how credible each report is, and what we think Apple is likely to announce and when.


Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
Late 2026 planned
Early 2027 a possibility
While Apple has yet to officially confirm the device, reports from respected analysts, supply-chain sources, and references discovered in Apple’s software all suggest development is well underway. The company is widely expected to launch a redesigned MacBook Pro featuring its first touchscreen OLED display in either late 2026 or early 2027.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Earlier rumours pointed firmly to a launch in the second half of 2026. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.
However, a launch in early 2027 now appears more likely. Global DRAM and NAND shortages, which prompted Apple to raise Mac and iPad prices in June 2026 – are expected to continue well into 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into until early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule.
In a July report, Gurman reiterated that these laptops are planned for this fall, but a 2027 ship date is possible.
Taken together, the continuing component shortages, Apple’s revised silicon plans, and the scale of the redesign make early 2027 the more likely launch window, although a late 2026 release has not yet been ruled out.


						

							


Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen? 
Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips
Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.
Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.
For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.
The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design
Thinner than the current MacBook Pro
Punch hole for the FaceTime camera
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to arrive as part of the biggest redesign to Apple’s professional laptop lineup in years. According to multiple reports, Apple is working on a thinner, lighter MacBook Pro made possible by more efficient Apple silicon and OLED display technology.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2024 that Apple was planning to slim down the MacBook Pro. The current 14-inch MacBook Pro measures 0.61 inches (1.55cm) thick when closed, and while the redesigned model is expected to be noticeably thinner, it will likely remain slightly thicker than the MacBook Air to accommodate its more powerful hardware.
One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.
Other rumoured design changes include:
A thinner and lighter chassis.
OLED display technology.
A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.
These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.


						

							


Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?
M5 Pro and M5 Max
Early rumours suggested the touchscreen MacBook Pro would debut with Apple’s M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. However, more recent reports indicate that Apple has revised its plans and will instead launch the first touchscreen MacBook with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors before moving directly to the M7 generation.
According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple now plans to pair the redesigned MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than the previously rumoured M6 Pro and M6 Max. The report claims Apple may skip the M6 Pro/Max generation entirely to accelerate development of its AI-focused M7 chips, bringing them to market around six months earlier with significantly more powerful on-device AI capabilities.
While the ongoing DRAM and NAND shortages may also have influenced the decision, they are not thought to be the primary reason for the roadmap change. Apple has already raised Mac and iPad prices in response to higher memory costs.
The latest reports supersede earlier rumours that the touchscreen MacBook would feature M6-series processors built on TSMC’s 2nm process with a redesigned chip architecture. Leaked Apple files discovered by MacRumors in late 2025 also appeared to reference M6 MacBook Pro models, suggesting Apple was developing M6-based hardware before reportedly changing direction.
Separately, there has also been speculation that Apple could introduce its in-house 5G modem to a future MacBook Pro, enabling cellular connectivity without requiring Wi-Fi or an iPhone hotspot. However, this remains one of the least substantiated rumours surrounding the redesign.
Omdia predicted that the touchscreen MacBook would have an M5 Ultra chip, but that prediction doesn’t seem to be based on any information. The M5 Ultra is used in the Mac Studio, which can accommodate the hardware cooling system the Ultra chip needs. A laptop isn’t capable of supporting such an elaborate system. Omdia has since removed its report with the prediction from its website.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Display
Tandem OLED display
Touchscreen interface
This redesigned model is anticipated to feature a major display overhaul, transitioning to an OLED panel that will likely offer a slimmer form factor similar to the iPad Pro
The display is expected to be the headline upgrade of Apple’s redesigned MacBook Pro. Multiple reports suggest Apple will replace the current Liquid Retina XDR (mini-LED) panel with a touchscreen OLED display, bringing MacBook Pro technology closer to the Ultra Retina XDR display used in the latest iPad Pro.
According to analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, Apple is planning to introduce OLED touch panels in the MacBook Pro in late 2026 or early 2027. The new display is expected to be thinner, more power-efficient, and capable of delivering deeper blacks, higher contrast, richer colours, and improved HDR performance than today’s mini-LED screens.
Reports indicate that both the 14-inch and 16-inch models will use advanced tandem OLED technology, which combines two OLED layers to achieve higher brightness levels while maintaining excellent energy efficiency. Apple first introduced this technology with the M4 iPad Pro and is expected to bring a similar implementation to the MacBook Pro.
The touchscreen functionality will reportedly rely on on-cell touch technology, which integrates touch sensors directly into the display rather than adding a separate layer. This approach helps keep the panel thin while supporting multi-touch input.
If the rumours prove accurate, the move to a tandem OLED touchscreen would represent the biggest display upgrade in the MacBook Pro’s history and one of the most significant changes to the lineup in years.

				
					

				
			
The iPad Pro has a Tadem OLED display, the type of display that could make its way into the 2026 MacBook Pro.

Brady Snyder / Foundry



							


Touchscreen MacBook Interface 

				
					

				
			
macOS 27 coming later in 2026 could have some hidden touchscreen features. 

Foundry




Apple is not expected to turn macOS into iPadOS, but reports suggest macOS 27 could include subtle design changes to make the Mac easier to use with touch input.
Rather than replacing the traditional desktop experience, Apple is reportedly working on a touch-tuned interface that adapts depending on how the device is being used. When touch input is detected, interface elements such as menus, buttons, and controls may automatically enlarge to make them easier to tap. When using a mouse or trackpad, macOS would revert to its familiar point-and-click layout.
The touchscreen itself is expected to support standard gestures such as tapping, scrolling, and zooming, while still allowing users to switch between touch, trackpad, and mouse input.
Apple didn’t announce touchscreen Mac support outright at WWDC, but the preview of macOS 27 and subsequent beta has offered clues about how the company plans to make macOS more touch-friendly while keeping the MacBook and iPad lines distinct.
There has also been speculation that Apple could update the trackpad with a new sensor layer to support Apple Pencil features such as hover or writing, possibly alongside a wider trackpad aimed at creative workflows.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Connectivity 
5G connectivity could finally come to the Mac

				
					

				
			The C1X is now available,  but the C2 modem could be ready for the 2026 MacBook Pro.
Apple




Beyond the touchscreen display and redesigned chassis, one of the most intriguing rumours surrounding the next-generation MacBook Pro is built-in cellular connectivity.
Apple has spent the past several years developing its own modem technology, beginning with the C-series modem family. Reports suggest the company has explored bringing 5G connectivity to the MacBook lineup, allowing users to connect directly to mobile networks without relying on Wi-Fi or a smartphone hotspot.
Further evidence emerged in 2025 when Macworld contributor Filipe Esposito reported that Apple had tested an M5 MacBook Pro equipped with a 5G modem. While that feature did not make it into the final product, the report suggests Apple is actively evaluating cellular-enabled MacBooks.
The redesigned MacBook Pro could also benefit from Apple’s growing portfolio of wireless chips. The company’s N-series networking processors, which handle Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Thread connectivity, may eventually replace third-party components throughout the Mac lineup. An updated version of the chip could debut alongside the touchscreen MacBook Pro, improving power efficiency and tighter integration with Apple’s ecosystem.
While neither feature has been confirmed, Apple’s ongoing investment in modem and wireless technologies makes enhanced connectivity one of the more plausible additions to the redesigned MacBook Pro.


						

							


Touchscreen MacBook Pro: Price expectations
Apple will likely offer similar configurations to the current MacBook Pro models, but it’s unclear how much of a premium a touchscreen OLED display will command. Apple upped the price of the iPad Pro by $200 when it got a tandem OLED, so it’s likely the touchscreen MacBook Pro will have a higher starting price.
Here are the prices for the current standard configurations of the M5 MacBook Pro, which saw prices increase between $300 and $500 in June 2026.
14-inch MacBook Pro
$1,999/£1,999: M5 with a 10-core CPU, 10-core GPU, 16GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 4
$2,499/£2,499: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,099/£4,099: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
16-inch MacBook Pro
$2,999/£2,999: M5 Pro with a 15-core CPU, 16-core GPU, 24GB unified memory, 1TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5
$4,399/£4,399: M5 Max with a 18-core CPU, 32-core GPU, 36GB unified memory, 2TB SSD, Thunderbolt 5

title: 2026 iPad mini guide: OLED, A19 Pro and price rumors
content:
Macworld





For those who need a premium small-screen tablet, the iPad mini is a popular choice. But should you buy one now, or should you wait to see what Apple has in store for the next model? 
Most buyers should wait – the next model is expected to bring meaningful upgrades. However, Apple isn’t expected to update the iPad mini until late 2026, and that launch date could slip further due to chip demand and wider supply constraints.
Here’s what the latest rumors say about the release date, key upgrades, and whether it’s worth waiting. 
2026 iPad mini: Rumored changes at a glance
A19 Pro (possibly A20 Pro)
Possible OLED display upgrade
Screen size could increase from 8.3-inch to 8.5- or 8.7-inches
More water-resistant design
Vibration-based speaker system
Price increase
Improved connectivity 


2026 iPad mini release date: When will the new iPad mini launch?
October 2026 is the reported timeframe
Apple has not officially announced a specific launch date for a new iPad mini. However, industry analysis and leaks suggest that a refresh is likely to occur before the end of 2026. In October 2025, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that a new iPad mini featuring an OLED screen is among the devices Apple is expected to launch before the end of 2026. In July 2026, Gurman reported that the OLED iPad mini is scheduled for an October 2026 release.
In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the iPad mini in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
Several reports state that the macOS 26.7 release candidate includes references to the upcoming iPad mini. This confirms that a new iPad mini is planned, but the release date has yet to be established.
Several factors could influence the timing of its release and cause delays, though, including: 
Erratic release cycle: The iPad mini doesn’t follow a fixed update schedule and can go several years between refreshes. While some reports suggest Apple is aiming for a “sooner-than-later” update to bring it in line with newer chips, its history of two-year (or longer) gaps suggests another update isn’t imminent following the October 2024 model.
Component shortages: Apple’s plans may be affected by demand for the A18 Pro chip expected to power the device. This processor also powers the hugely popular MacBook Neo, which has led to reports that Apple could prioritise these chips for the Neo over the iPad mini. In addition, there are industry-wide supply pressures affecting RAM and other components which Apple CEO Tim Cook alluded to during the company’s first-quarter 2026 results announcement. 


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Performance and specs 
A19 Pro chip
C1X modem
N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6
Since it hasn’t been updated in over a year, the next iPad mini is expected to receive several silicon upgrades. The current model features an A17 Pro chip, 8GB of RAM, and Apple Intelligence support. Most rumors suggest Apple will upgrade the device to the A19 Pro.
In August 2025, MacRumors reported that Apple code inadvertently revealed an A19 Pro-powered iPad mini, although the publication noted that the chip could also have been intended for the iPhone Air. Additional evidence emerged in December 2025, when Macworld reported seeing internal Apple code indicating that the entry-level iPad would launch with an A19 chip. Because Apple has traditionally equipped the iPad mini with a more powerful processor than the standard iPad, this lends further support to the A19 Pro rumor.
An A19 Pro would represent a substantial upgrade over the current A17 Pro. Users could expect faster on-device AI processing, improved gaming performance, and quicker photo and video editing. The A18 Pro, which powers the MacBook Neo, is often compared to the M1 chip and can rival the M3 in some single-core workloads. An A19 Pro-powered iPad mini would push the device even closer to iPad Air-level performance.
There are also reports that Apple could use the A20 Pro in the iPad mini instead. The likely chip may depend on launch timing. If the new iPad mini arrives before the iPhone 18 Pro, which is expected to debut the A20 Pro, the A19 Pro remains the most likely option. However, if the launch slips into late 2026 or beyond, an A20 Pro-equipped iPad mini becomes increasingly plausible.
A less ambitious upgrade to the A18 Pro remains possible. While the performance gains would be smaller, the chip still offers meaningful improvements over the A17 Pro thanks to architectural enhancements and a more powerful GPU configuration. In benchmarks, it would outperform the current model, though the difference would be less dramatic than with an A19 Pro or A20 Pro.
The popularity of the MacBook Neo could also influence Apple’s chip strategy. Reports suggest demand for the Neo has been strong enough to create pressure on A18 Pro supply, which could affect the availability of chips for other products.
Alongside processor upgrades, Apple is expected to bring its latest wireless technologies to the iPad mini. With the iPhone 17 lineup, Apple introduced the N1 chip, which supports Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The company has already added the N1 to the M4 iPad Air and is expected to roll it out across the iPad lineup through 2026 and 2027, including the iPad mini. Cellular models are also expected to adopt Apple’s C1X modem.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Display
OLED display upgrade

				
					

				
			
The M4 iPad Pro’s OLED Display could make its way to the iPad mini next.

Mahmoud Itani / Foundry




The biggest display upgrade rumored for the next iPad mini is the adoption of OLED technology. Following Apple’s transition of the iPad Pro to OLED in 2024, multiple reports have suggested that the iPad mini will be the next iPad to make the switch. Ross Young of DSCC was first to claim, in a tweet in October 2024, that the next iPad mini would have a OLED. 
The current iPad mini, released in October 2024, still uses a Liquid Retina IPS LCD display, but industry sources, including Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, indicate a move to OLED is increasingly likely.
The transition from LCD to OLED would represent one of the most significant upgrades in the iPad mini’s history. Unlike LCD panels, which rely on a backlight, OLED displays illuminate each pixel individually. This allows pixels to switch off completely when displaying black content, resulting in deeper blacks, higher contrast ratios, and improved HDR performance.
Key benefits of OLED include:
Superior contrast and true blacks: Individual pixel control delivers inky blacks and virtually infinite contrast.
More vibrant colours: OLED panels typically offer wider colour gamuts and greater colour accuracy, producing richer and more immersive images.
Faster response times: Reduced motion blur and ghosting improve the experience when gaming or watching fast-moving content.
Better viewing angles: Colours and brightness remain consistent even when viewed from the side.
Improved efficiency: OLED can be more power-efficient when displaying darker content and allows for thinner display assemblies.
An OLED panel could also enable Apple to reduce bezel sizes, potentially increasing the display area slightly without significantly changing the tablet’s overall dimensions. Some reports suggest the screen could grow from 8.3 inches to around 8.5 inches as a result – more on that below.
While the iPad mini is unlikely to inherit premium display technologies such as ProMotion or the tandem OLED architecture used in the iPad Pro, the move to OLED would still deliver a noticeable improvement in visual quality, with richer blacks, better contrast, improved colour reproduction, and stronger HDR performance.
For users who prioritise display quality, an OLED iPad mini would address one of the most frequently cited limitations of the current model and bring the compact tablet much closer to the viewing experience offered by Apple’s premium devices.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Design
Same size, bigger screen possible
More water-resistant design rumored

				
					

				
			
Apple




The iPad mini has retained the same design since its major redesign in 2021, and the 2026 model is expected to keep that overall look. However, Apple could increase the display size slightly while maintaining the device’s current dimensions.
In December 2024, analysts at Display Supply Chain Consultants (DSCC) suggested in a supply chain analyst report that the next-generation iPad mini could feature an 8.5-inch display, up from the current model’s 8.3-inch panel. The reports indicated that the chassis size would remain unchanged, meaning Apple could achieve the larger screen through slimmer bezels rather than a larger body.
A larger display may also help the iPad mini maintain its place in Apple’s lineup as foldable devices arrive. Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone – often referred to as the iPhone Fold or iPhone Ultra – is expected to feature an inner display measuring between 7.6 and 7.8 inches with a 4:3 aspect ratio, putting it close to the iPad mini’s screen size. While still smaller than the iPad mini, such a device could appeal to some users who currently favour Apple’s smallest tablet. 
Another rumor gaining traction is that the new iPad mini will be more water-resistant. That rumor comes from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who in October 2025 claimed Apple was developing a next-generation iPad mini with a significantly more water-resistant chassis. 
The design changes could include: 
Redesigned casing with improved sealing around ports. 
A new speaker system that uses vibration-based audio technology to eliminate traditional speaker holes. 
There’s also a strong possibility of new colour options. Apple currently offers the iPad mini in Blue, Purple, Starlight, and Space Gray, while the previous generation was available in Pink, Purple, Starlight, and Space Gray.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Cameras 
Little or no camera upgrade expected

				
					

				
			
Apple is not expected to upgrade the cameras in the next iPad mini.

Foundry




Apple’s iPads currently feature a 12MP Center Stage front-facing camera and a 12MP wide rear camera, and there are no credible reports suggesting major camera system upgrades for the next iPad mini. 
The most likely change concerns camera placement rather than camera hardware. Apple has moved the front-facing camera to the landscape edge on its latest iPad models, and the iPad mini could follow suit to improve the experience during video calls and FaceTime sessions when used with a keyboard or stand.
While the cameras themselves may remain unchanged, image quality could still benefit from improvements to the image signal processor and computational photography capabilities of a newer A-series chip.


						

							


2026 iPad mini: Price 
The iPad mini has had the same $499 price tag since its 2021 redesign. In 2026 we could see a price increase as a result of the OLED display upgrade. 
Component costs could also drive up the price. During Apple’s first quarter 2026 financial results announcement, CEO Tim Cook said that Apple is now “in a supply chase mode” due to industry-wide constraints. Thus, tariffs, the rising cost of RAM, and other increases in supply-chain costs could impact pricing for some higher-end storage options.
The price may remain the same though, with Apple wanting to keep the price of this niche product attractive.

title: Apple Reportedly Plans to Release These 14 Products by Early Next Year
content:
Apple will be holding its next event on Wednesday, September 9 to unveil its latest iPhones and Apple Watches, but that is not all, according to a new report.


Bloomberg's Mark Gurman today shared a long list of products that he expects Apple to unveil between next week and early 2027.

Our list below summarizes Gurman's reporting and mixes in some other rumors.

iPhones


iPhone 18 Pro: A20 Pro chip, a smaller Dynamic Island, a simplified Camera Control button, new Dark Cherry and Light Blue color options, improved vapor chambers to prevent overheating, and more.

iPhone 18 Pro Max: The same features rumored for the iPhone 18 Pro, but the Pro Max model may be slightly thicker due to a larger battery and a variable aperture camera, which might be exclusive to the Pro Max model this year.

iPhone Ultra: A foldable so-called "iPhone Ultra" with a 7.7-inch inner display and 5.3-inch outer display, two rear 48-megapixel Wide and Ultra Wide cameras, one front camera, a Touch ID power button instead of Face ID, an A20 Pro chip, and more. The device's crease is expected to be less noticeable compared to many previous foldables. iOS 27 will have more landscape apps, side-by-side apps, and other multitasking features on the device. Expect to spend $2,000 or more.

Apple Watches

Apple Watch Series 12: A faster S11 chip or newer, longer battery life, and a ceramic case option. Fitness tracking improvements may include a continuous heart-rate sensor that can run the whole day, even outside of workouts.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: A faster S11 chip or newer, fitness tracking improvements such as the continuous heart-rate sensor, and additional satellite features for the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and newer, such as Apple Maps via satellite and the ability to send and receive photos with Messages via satellite.
Touch ID was initially rumored for the next Apple Watches but has seemingly been ruled out.
iPads

iPad mini: A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip, an OLED display, a vibration-based speaker system, and a water-resistant design.


Macs


iMac: M6 chip and new color options. Apple announced the M6 chip last week.

MacBook Pro: A new 14-inch MacBook Pro base model with an M6 chip.

MacBook Ultra: A major MacBook Pro redesign in late 2026 or early 2027, with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, an OLED display, a touch screen, a Dynamic Island, and a thinner design. On this laptop, which will reportedly be named MacBook Ultra, macOS 27 is expected to offer a touch-friendly interface. While this rumor is far less certain, it has also been said that it might be possible to configure the MacBook Ultra with the M5 Ultra chip that debuted last week.

Home


Apple TV: At least five new features, including an A17 Pro chip or newer, an increased 8GB of RAM for Apple Intelligence, Siri AI support, an Apple-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and an updated Siri Remote. The new Apple TV will apparently look similar to the existing model, so do not expect any major design changes.

HomePod mini: Newer chip with Siri AI support, improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and potentially new color options like red. The new HomePod mini will apparently look similar to the existing model, so do not expect any major design changes.

Home Hub: An all-new smart home hub featuring Siri AI, a 6-inch to 7-inch square display, an A18 chip or newer for Apple Intelligence, FaceTime, and more. A new operating system will feature clock faces, widgets, and more. There will a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version.

Headphones

AirPods 5: Two new AirPods 5 models with and without active noise cancellation.

Beats 360: New over-ear Beats 360 headphones with an AirPods Max-like design, interchangeable ear cushions and headbands, up to 1.75× more noise cancellation than the Beats Studio Pro, IPX4-rated water resistance, and more.

title: The M6 MacBook Pro is coming. Is it worth waiting for?
content:
Macworld





Apple offers the MacBook Pro with three different chip options. It starts with the entry-level M5 chip, which you can only get in the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple also offers higher end M5 Pro and M5 Max chips for the 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro, as it has since the M1 arrived in 2020.
The M5 MacBook Pro was released in October 2025. According to reports, Apple plans to upgrade the laptop to an M6 chip this fall, which isn’t a surprise. What is a surprise is that Apple will reportedly skip the Pro and Max M6 variants to focus on the M7 coming later in 2027. So the M6 MacBook Pro could be the only M6 option available.
This article keeps track of the reports about the upcoming M6 MacBook Pro. Keep an eye on this article for the latest news.


M6 MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
• Fall 2026 expected
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the M6 MacBook Pro in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.
In a July report, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the M6 MacBook Pro is expected to ship this fall. Of the five generations of the entry-level MacBook Pro, three have been released in the October/November timeframe, including the past two releases. Here are the release dates for the entry-level MacBook Pro:
M5 MacBook Pro: October 2025
M4 MacBook Pro: November 2024
M3 MacBook Pro: January 2023
M2 MacBook Pro: June 2022
M1 MacBook Pro: November 2020
This release could be affected by the memory chip shortage that has been affecting the whole tech industry. If Apple is unable to obtain the quantity of chips it needs, Apple could be forced to move the release date back. Or, there could have a short supply of laptops available, which would result in actual delivery dates slipping.
At this point in time, we haven’t heard of any delays. The fall release of the M6 MacBook Pro seems to be on schedule, but the volatility of the chip market could cause it to change unexpectedly.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Chip details
First 2nm M-series chip
Redesigned GPU
Apple will upgrade the MacBook Pro M5 to an M6 chip, which will be the key upgrade for this release cycle. The chip is expected to be the first M-series chip built using TSMC’s 2nm process. A smaller process allows for more transistors to be placed on the chip, which would result in faster speeds and improved power efficiency.

				
					

				
			
The M6 chip is expected to incorporate new features for improved AI processing.

Apple




The M5 chip comes with 10 CPU cores: 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores. No reports have been made about the M6 CPU core count, but Gurman reported that “performance will also improve.” Apple is also planning enhancements for the built-in video codecs. 
In June, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the M6 could offer an updated memory architecture and memory bandwidth of 200 GB/s, a 31 percent increase over the M5’s 153 GB/s. Apple will also likely update the chip’s Neural Engine to help AI processing for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. As for the RAM configurations, Apple offers the M5 with 16GB, 24GB, or 32GB of RAM. Apple isn’t expected to change this with the M6.
The M6 will also have a redesigned GPU. Gurman reported that Apple tested a version of the M6 with 12 GPU cores, which is two more than the M5.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Other specifications and features
No major changes expected
The chip upgrade to the M6 is expected to be the only major change with the back MacBook Pro release. The display, keyboard, trackpad, ports, and other features are all expected to be identical or similar to the M5 MacBook Pro.

				
					

				
			
The M6 MacBook Pro could be the last entry-level model of this particular design.

Foundry




According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is planning an entry-level M7 MacBook Pro for 2027. This laptop will have a base M7 chip that replaces the M6, but it will also have several new features to match those introduced with the touchscreen MacBook Pro. The entry-level  M7 MacBook Pro will have a new design, an OLED display, and other features, but it’s not expected to have a touchscreen.


						

							


M6 MacBook Pro: Price
$1,999 (expected)
Ongoing memory constraints could affect configurations
We haven’t heard any reports about the price of the entry-level M6 MacBook Pro, but we can look at recent price history to get an idea. When the M5 MacBook Pro was released in 2025, its starting price was $1,599. Apple bumped it to $1,699 when the M5 Pro and Max models arrived earlier this year and increased the starting storage to 1TB. This past June, however, Apple raised the price to $1,999 due to supply chain constraints. Those constraints aren’t going away anytime soon, and it’s likely that the higher price is now the new normal.
During Apple’s Q3 2026 financial announcement in July, Apple CEO Tim Cook and CFO Kevan Parekh made it a point to explain that the supply chain constraints will affect production costs for months to come. ” We expect the impact from supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” said Parekh. “The projected supply constraints in the September quarter affect iPhone, Mac, and iPad.” Cook said, “With less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially.”
With this in mind, it’s quite possible that prices could go up again with the release of the M6 MacBook Pro. It’s unlikely, but the state of the chip supply chain will influence what prices Apple will offer.
Considering that the M7 MacBook Pro won’t be far from replacing the yet-to-be-released M6 MacBook Pro, one strategy Apple could employ is to price the M6 MacBook Pro at the same $1,999 price and push any price hikes to the next generation. If that’s the case, the M6 could be a good option for anyone on the fence about upgrading.

title: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders might start later this year
content:
Macworld





Just a few days ago, Apple announced the date for its annual Phone event: Wednesday, September 9, less than two weeks away. We’re expecting Apple to unveil its first-ever folding iPhone at the event, along with the iPhone 18 Pro and Apple Watch Series 12. But if you’re looking to buy one of them, you might have to wait longer than usual.
A reliable source has told Macwelt that pre-orders this year are not set to begin, as usual, on the Friday following the launch. Instead, Apple will open pre-orders a day later, on Saturday, September 12. The reason for this is that this year, September 11 falls on the Friday following the event, a day of remembrance and mourning in the U.S.
The time is also set to change, according to the source: While pre-orders usually begin at 5 am PT, Apple is reportedly opening up pre-sales at midnight PT on Saturday. Apple held midnight PT pre-orders until the iPhone 11, when it shifted the time to better accommodate other time zones.
It wouldn’t be the first time Apple has moved pre-orders from Friday to the following Saturday: 11 years ago, the iPhone 6S and 6S Plus weren’t available for pre-order until Saturday, September 12, 2015, for the same reason. 
This preorder should apply to the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and any other surprises Apple has in store. However, if you’re looking to buy one of the foldable iPhone Ultras, reports claim that preorders might not begin until late September. A similar situation occurred in 2020, when the iPhone 12 Mini and the iPhone 12 Pro Max were launched later than the iPhone 12 and the iPhone 12 Pro due to the coronavirus pandemic. Apple also delayed the iPhone X in 2017 due to production issues with the next-gen handset.

title: Ugreen Launches HomeAgent AI Hubs and Liquid-Cooled Qi2 Charger
content:
Consumer technology maker Ugreen has announced HomeAgent, its first smart home platform, combining security camera storage, on-device AI, and Matter-based device control in a single hub. 


The hub is capable of processing and storing camera footage, files, and other media with no monthly storage fee. Ugreen says the onboard AI can also identify people, vehicles, pets, and packages in footage, as well as summarize events and search recorded video by keyword. 

The hub is then able to create highlight reels from camera footage as well as stored photo libraries, and it can display them on Ugreen's Gallery LCD Smart Frames.  

The hub works as a Matter controller and can talk to third-party devices over Wi-Fi, Zigbee, Thread, Bluetooth, NFC, ONVIF/RTSP, and PoE. Ugreen's compatibility list includes devices from Aqara, ThirdReality, SwitchBot, and Eve, with the company promising more third-party support to come, though the initial phase is limited to lights, switches, sensors, and curtains.

All of this can be controlled by talking to the onboard AI assistant Uliya, which can also check live status or event history, and can generate voice notifications for events like packages arriving or the sound of a baby crying.

The hub is available in three configurations, each with increasing levels of AI processing power. The entry-level HA100 comes with storage, camera security, and device control, and responds to voice commands, while the HA100 Pro offers faster network connectivity and more compute for heavier workloads. 


Then there's the MasterAgent Ma100, which runs on NVIDIA's Jetson Thor T5000 platform. Ugreen says it runs at up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of local compute and calls it the hub for larger models juggling multiple devices and tasks at once.

Ugreen's website, with a $50 deposit securing 50% off ahead of a Kickstarter campaign that starts on October 27. Early bird pricing for the three models is $899, $2,999, and $9,999, respectively.

Elsewhere, Ugreen has also launched a 25W MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank, featuring a 10,000mAh battery. The company is touting it as the world's first liquid-cooled Qi2 power bank, since it features a micro-pump that circulates coolant behind a transparent window, so you can actually watch it flowing around inside. 


The MagFlow Pro costs $149.99 and is available now from Ugreen and Amazon.

title: Apple’s iPhone Ultra color options won’t include black, sources say
content:
Macworld





In Cupertino, it seems like blue is the new black. After the iPhone 17 Pro skipped black for a Deep Blue hue, the MacBook Neo followed in the Midnight MacBook Air’s footsteps with Indigo as the only darker option. And now we expect its first folding phone, dubbed the iPhone Ultra, to take a similar path when it is introduced next week.
As we reported earlier this year, the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will come in two new colors when they’re unveiled at Apple’s Surprise and Shine event next week. The flagship color will be Dark Cherry, which has a purplish hue. It is expected to be joined by Light Blue, somewhat reminiscent of the iPhone 13 Pro’s Sierra Blue. We also expect there will be silver and dark gray options, though it’s possible only one will make the final cut.
For the folding iPhone Ultra, however, the color options will be somewhat less… colorful. The same sources that told us about the iPhone 18 Pro colors also revealed the options for the folding iPhone Ultra, and they’re not what most people would expect.
When Apple introduced the radically redesigned iPhone X back in 2017, it was available in two options: silver and space gray. We assumed a similar set of options would be available for the iPhone Ultra, but our source says Apple will release the folding iPhone in two varieties: a standard silver-and-white model and a surprising Indigo Blue option. Our sources say the hue will be closer to the iPhone 17 Pro’s Deep Blue than the MacBook Neo, however.
Those colors were corroborated a few months later by known leaker Sonny Dickson, who shared a photo of the iPhone Ultra’s camera protectors in silver and dark blue.
Apple is expected to unveil the folding iPhone Ultra at its Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday at 10 am PT. title: Your wallet can sit out this week’s Apple event
content:
Macworld





On September 9, Apple is scheduled to hold its most anticipated hardware-centric event of the year. During the “Surprise and shine” keynote, Apple CEO John Ternus is expected to announce the all-new iPhone Ultra, alongside iPhone 18 Pro models, fresh Apple Watches, enhanced AirPods, and an overhauled smart home line. 
While many of these devices will pack new hardware with a lot of hype behind it, it may be wise to skip buying your annual Apple upgrade this fall. Not only will iPhones be more expensive than ever, but many of the upgrades we’re expecting might not be worthy of an upgrade at all.
Insufficiently Ultra
Perhaps the event’s most exciting announcement will be the iPhone Ultra. The first-generation product will mark Apple’s entry into the foldable market, rivaling Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the like. It’ll probably offer some neat benefits, like a more powerful iOS multitasking system and the ability to seamlessly switch between the small and large screen form factors. Essentially, it’s a hybrid device that blends an iPhone with an iPad mini. It all sounds great until you take a closer look at the full package.

				
					

				
			
Ice Universe




Despite its rumored Ultra branding, the foldable will sacrifice several iPhone features available on cheaper models. Most notably, it’ll downgrade biometric authentication from Face ID to Touch ID and exclude the telephoto camera that enables a longer zoom range. It may also come in just two lifeless colorways.
Taking its high cost into consideration, it’s hard to justify buying the iPhone Ultra. It’s usually advisable to steer clear of first-gen devices, especially when they cost $2,000-2,500 and aren’t as capable as the rest of the lineup. I’d recommend waiting for its successor, which will almost surely address some of the original iPhone Ultra’s shortcomings and potentially be more durable. Until then, using an iPhone and iPad separately provides a wider feature set and a longer combined battery life.
Familiar Pro-file
With the iPhone Ultra out of the way, you may be eyeing an iPhone 18 Pro instead. After all, the Pro models are the most advanced and reliable of their kind, offering Apple’s latest innovations in the mobile department. Nevertheless, you’ll want to skip that, too.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro will likely introduce three core changes: a faster A20 Pro processor, a smaller Dynamic Island cutout, and new finishes. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could solely get a variable aperture lens that helps elevate photography. While welcome, these upgrades will come at a cost, as the devices will reportedly see a $100-300 price hike. For most users, it’s wiser to buy a more fairly priced iPhone 17 Pro or wait for next year’s iPhone XX, which should be a dramatic overhaul that arguably warrants the upcharge.
Watch from afar
Beyond the new iPhones, the company is expected to announce the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 during its upcoming event. The smartwatches could feature the first performance boost in three years and an all-day heart rate monitor. There have also been some rumors about ceramic editions of the Series variants and an updated fitness tracking system.
But here’s the thing—all models from the Apple Watch Series 9 already support all of watchOS 27’s announced features, including Siri AI. They also continuously record your heart rate while you exercise and, otherwise, periodically do so throughout the day. That’s enough relevant data collection to give users a solid idea of their overall cardiovascular state. As for the refreshed fitness system, that will presumably be a watchOS 27 software perk that expands to all compatible models—not just the latest ones.
As such, if you use an Apple Watch Series 9 or newer, it’s best to skip upgrading this year and wait for the noticeably redesigned model rumored to launch as soon as next year.
Sound decision
Other mobile accessories I expect to see at the event are two AirPods 5 variants. Like the AirPods 4, the latest-generation wearable will provide optional active noise cancellation (ANC) for those willing to pay a bit more. Given that Apple typically offers its best audio technology in the AirPods Pro line, it’s unlikely that the AirPods 5 will introduce any meaningful features unavailable on AirPods Pro 3. The refresh could be largely iterative, focusing on connectivity improvements and battery life. For something more exciting, I advise waiting for the camera-equipped AirPods rumored to debut in 2027, as they’ll enable major new capabilities.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Smart spending
Apart from mobile devices, the “Surprise and shine” event will possibly feature Apple’s biggest smart home push to date. The Apple TV 4K and HomePod could leverage faster chips to unlock Siri AI. But let’s face it—your current smart speakers and set-top boxes can play music and movies just fine. While Siri AI is nice to have, it’s not an essential feature for media streaming devices.

				
					

				
			
Foundry




More importantly, Apple could reveal its first-ever dedicated smart home hub, which some are calling the HomePad. The new device will use a new OS with a new interface, letting you easily view your smart home’s state and control HomeKit and Matter accessories. It’ll likely also support FaceTime calls, viewing News+ recipes, and other existing Apple services. Despite that, I still fail to see its unique selling point. The Apple TV 4K and HomePod already act as HomeKit hubs to power automations, remote control, and more. 
iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and even watchOS all support interacting with smart accessories using the built-in Home app. Unless its exclusive use cases haven’t leaked yet, I see little reason why one would add a HomePad to their setup.

title: Apple Is Testing a Four-HomePod Surround System, Code Suggests
content:
Apple appears to be working on some major new HomePod home theater features, including a four-speaker surround sound system and a new "Party Mode," according to code found in audioOS 27 beta 8, and shared on the MacRumors forums by member pdfu.


References in the software for the second-generation HomePod suggest the ability to tune for a setup with front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right HomePods. The four-speaker surround configuration references automatic room calibration, speaker-position mapping, timing adjustments, bass management, EQ, dialogue enhancement, and different processing modes for movies and music.

For stereo content, the code suggests the ability to either spatialize sound across all four speakers or limit traditional stereo playback to the two front speakers.

The files also reference a new tuning system called "Forklift" that combines two second-generation HomePods with two speakers that use an unidentified AID12007 hardware family. We haven't seen this identifier before – it doesn't correspond to any existing HomePod models – suggesting it refers to a future HomePod mini, third-generation HomePod, or some other unreleased audio device.

In addition, Apple appears to be working on a new "Party Mode" feature for stereo-paired HomePods. The feature applies a more diffuse sound field that's designed to spread sound more evenly across the room for a more immersive listening experience, rather than optimizing playback for a single listening position.

The Home app and Apple TV do not currently provide a way to configure four HomePods as a surround system. Indeed, none of these features have been referenced before. All we can say at this point is that they indicate that Apple is testing them, but whether Apple ultimately releases them remains to be seen. 

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, so it's possible that these features could be part of Apple's broader Home refresh. Watch this space.

title: Five Sleeps Until iPhone 18 Pro: Here's What We Know
content:
We are just five sleeps away from Apple's unveiling of its new-generation iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models, not forgetting its first foldable iPhone.


Apple is expected to introduce the devices at its annual iPhone fall event, which is this year carrying the tagline "Surprise and shine." The event takes place on Wednesday, September 9. To help you get some shuteye in the meantime, here's a rundown of the features we're expecting from Apple's iPhone 18 Pro models.

Overall Design: The iPhone 18 Pro models are expected to stick to the overall iPhone 17 Pro design, but they could feature a more seamless rear casing with less contrast between the glass and aluminum frame.

Battery Life: The iPhone 18 Pro Max is rumored to feature a larger 5,100–5,200 mAh battery and a slightly thicker, heavier design as a result.

Smaller Dynamic Island: Apple is expected to shrink the Dynamic Island, made possible by moving some Face ID components beneath the display.

Upgraded Display: The iPhone 18 Pro models are said to use a more power-efficient LTPO+ display, supplied by Samsung Display and LG Display.

A20 Pro Chip: Apple's next-generation chip will use TSMC's advanced 2nm process, including Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which should bring improvements to performance and power efficiency.

C2 Modem: Apple's next-generation in-house cellular modem could feature in the Pro models, offering faster speeds, and improved efficiency. However, it's possible the C2 still lacks mmWave capability, and that the devices will use a Qualcomm modem in the United States and Apple's C2 modem in other parts of the world.

New Camera Sensor: Samsung is believed to have developed a new three-layer stacked image sensor for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup that improves responsiveness, noise, and dynamic range.

Variable Aperture: The 48-megapixel Fusion camera on both iPhone 18 Pro models is expected to gain a variable aperture for greater control over light and depth of field.

5G Satellite Internet: The iPhone 18 Pro models could support full 5G connectivity via satellite, which would be quite an expansion of Apple's existing satellite-based emergency features.

Simplified Camera Control: Apple is said to have redesigned the Camera Control button to use pressure sensing without a separate capacitive layer, simply to reduce complexity and cost.

New Colors: Apple has reportedly tested several new finishes, but we're betting on these three: Light Blue, Dark Cherry, and Silver. We no longer expect a Black option.

iOS 27: The iPhone 18 Pro will ship with iOS 27 and its overhauled Siri AI experience, which includes onscreen awareness, personal context, web knowledge, and expanded Apple Intelligence features.

Apple has held its fall event in the first two weeks of September in each of the last several years, with new iPhones typically going on sale the following Friday. It has been rumored that iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max pre-orders will begin on Saturday, September 12 at 12 a.m. Pacific Time this year.

title: M6 vs. M5 Pro Mac Mini Buyer's Guide
content:
Apple last week announced two new Mac mini models, one with the all-new M6 chip and one with the M5 Pro chip that debuted in the MacBook Pro earlier this year.


Somewhat like the ‌MacBook Pro‌ last year, Apple has again placed its newest silicon in the entry-level machine and a previous-generation Pro chip in the high-end machine, so the more expensive ‌Mac mini‌ is not simply a faster version of the cheaper one. The M6 model starts at $899 with a 12-core CPU, 16GB of unified memory, and 256GB of storage. The M5 Pro model starts at $1,699 with a 15-core CPU, 24GB of memory, and 512GB of storage, and it can be configured with up to an 18-core CPU and a 20-core GPU.

highest starting prices Apple has ever set for the ‌Mac mini‌, which makes the $800 gap between the two models more consequential than in previous generations. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these two ‌Mac mini‌ models is best for you.

available to pre-order now and launch on Tuesday, September 22. The two machines are physically identical and share the majority of their hardware. The shared features include:
 

The same 5.0 by 5.0 inch aluminum enclosure in silver, unchanged since 2024

Neural Accelerators in every GPU core, a first for the ‌Mac mini‌

Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via the N1 chip, another first for the ‌Mac mini‌ 

2.5Gb Ethernet as standard, with a 10Gb Ethernet configuration option

Two front USB-C ports and a headphone jack with high-impedance headphone support

An HDMI port and native support for up to three external displays

Genlock over USB-C for synchronizing a display with a camera such as the iPhone 17 Pro

macOS 27 with Apple Intelligence and Siri AI



Everything that differs between the two models is set out below:
 






‌Mac mini‌ (M6)
‌Mac mini‌ (M5 Pro)


M6 chip
M5 Pro chip


Built with TSMC's 2nm (N2) process
Built with TSMC's 3nm (N3P) process


12-core CPU
15-core or 18-core CPU


Two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores
Up to six super cores and 12 performance cores


World's fastest single-threaded performance, according to Apple



12-core GPU
16-core or 20-core GPU


Updated shader core architecture, Dynamic Caching, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing, with 50% higher geometry rates
Enhanced shader core with third-generation ray tracing


Dual 16-core Neural Engine, with up to 2x the peak compute of previous generations
16-core Neural Engine


Up to 170GB/s memory bandwidth
307GB/s memory bandwidth


16GB, 24GB, or 32GB of unified memory
24GB, 48GB, or 64GB of unified memory


256GB, 512GB, 1TB, or 2TB of storage
512GB, 1TB, 2TB, 4TB, or 8TB of storage


Three Thunderbolt 4 ports
Three Thunderbolt 5 ports



Clustering of multiple ‌Mac mini‌ systems over Thunderbolt 5


1.5 pounds (0.67 kg)
1.6 pounds (0.73 kg)


Starts at $899
Starts at $1,699




For the majority of buyers, the M6 model is the right choice, and not only because it is $800 cheaper. It is the newer chip, built on a 2nm process, and Apple says it contains the world's fastest CPU core. It is also the only ‌Mac mini‌ with the Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which Apple says delivers up to twice the peak compute of the single Neural Engine used in the M5 Pro. If your workload is dominated by everyday productivity, web work, photo editing, coding, or light on-device AI, the M6 should feel marginally faster in day-to-day use, especially for single-core tasks, and be more future-proof.
 
Buying the more expensive machine means accepting older silicon in exchange for a broader performance. What the M5 Pro provides is scale rather than speed per core: up to 18 CPU cores against 12, up to 20 GPU cores against 12, and 307GB/s of memory bandwidth against 170GB/s. Those advantages only really surface in sustained, heavily parallel work such as video rendering, 3D and VFX production, compilation of large codebases, and scientific simulation.
 
The memory ceiling is the clearest dividing line. The M6 model tops out at 32GB of unified memory, while the M5 Pro reaches 64GB. If you intend to run local large language models, work with complex 3D scenes, or keep sizeable datasets resident in memory, the M6 configuration simply cannot be specified high enough, no matter how much you spend on it. Storage works the same way, with the M6 limited to 2TB and the M5 Pro extending to 8TB.
 
Thunderbolt is the other hard limit. The M5 Pro model has three Thunderbolt 5 ports, double the bandwidth of the Thunderbolt 4 ports on the M6 model, and Thunderbolt 5 is what allows several ‌Mac mini‌ systems to be clustered together to run large AI models entirely on device. This is significant for users building a small local compute setup, or attaching high-speed external storage arrays for video work.
 
A note of caution applies to configuring the cheaper machine upward. Adding 32GB of memory and 2TB of storage to the M6 model pushes it well past its $899 starting price and narrows the gap to the M5 Pro considerably. At that point, the M5 Pro entry configuration becomes a more sensible purchase for anyone doing professional work, since the extra outlay buys substantially more CPU and GPU capacity, faster memory, and Thunderbolt 5 rather than just more of the same.
 
no plans for an M6 Pro chip, so the M5 Pro will remain the highest-end ‌Mac mini‌ option until the M7 family arrives in 2027. Buyers who want the newest Apple silicon in the smallest desktop Apple sells can only get it by choosing the $899 machine.

The Personal AI Router (PAIR) isn't hardware. Instead, it's software that connects supported Apple Silicon Macs, Nvidia RTX PCs, and DGX Spark systems.
PAIR works with Ollama and LM Studio, two tools for running AI models locally. It discovers participating computers and gives AI apps a single connection for sending requests, so users don't have to configure each app to reach every machine.
For someone already running local AI on a Mac, PAIR could put a compatible gaming PC to work when requests pile up. An AI agent reviewing several documents, for example, could have independent requests handled on different computers.

title: Wild report claims Apple might launch an M5 Ultra MacBook Pro
content:
Macworld





Reports about Apple switching its MacBooks and iPads to OLED displays have been circulating in the rumor mill for some time now. A new report by Omdia gives us a more concrete look at when the switch could actually happen, as well as a few far-out details about Apple’s alleged plans. [Omdia appears to have removed the report from its website.]
The first MacBook equipped with an OLED display will reportedly be available “by the end of 2026,” according to the site, which is in line with previous rumors. The MacBook Omdia is referring to is likely to be Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is expected later this year or in early 2027.
It appears, however, that the touchscreen MacBook will be a new addition to the MacBook Pro lineup, a higher-end model that could fall under Apple’s Ultra branding. Omdia states that “the existing 14.3-inch and 16.3-inch MacBook Pro models with LCD + Mini LED backlighting will not be discontinued,” which means the MacBook Pro lineup, as it is now, will continue, with Apple upgrading the chip on a regular basis.
Surprisingly, and perhaps unbelievably, Omdia predicts that this new model is “highly likely to be equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.” Apple’s M5 ultra chip is only used in the Mac Studio, which includes a complex thermal cooling system with a heavy copper heat sink that adds two pounds to the machine’s weight.
Omdia also reports that the MacBook Air will continue to use an LCD display, and that there’s a “new 13.8-inch MacBook, which is expected to launch in 2029 with a hybrid OLED display.” This “new” MacBook is likely an upgraded version of the MacBook Air, which has been reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman to be making the switch to OLED in the future.
Omida also confirms previous reports that an OLED iPad mini will arrive later this year. The current LCD iPad mini was released in October 2024, so it’s due for an update. It would be Apple’s first non-Pro tablet to have an OLED display.

title: Apple Reportedly Planning All-New MacBook Model Between Air and Pro
content:
Apple may introduce an entirely new 13.8-inch OLED MacBook model in 2029, potentially creating a new product tier between the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro, according to an updated product roadmap from research firm Omdia.


The firm's latest roadmap sandwiches a new 13.8-inch MacBook between the projected time line for the Air and Pro models. The surprise model is said to use a single-stack hybrid OLED panel, rather than the more sophisticated tandem OLED technology that is expected in the upcoming OLED MacBook Pro models, which are set to launch either later this year or early next year.

June report from ZDNet Korea, Apple sounded out Samsung Display, LG Display, and BOE for information regarding a 13.8-inch OLED MacBook panel earlier this year. At the time, the general assumption was that it was likely to be part of Apple's work on the first OLED MacBook Air, expected by 2028 at the earliest.

However, looking at Omdia's latest roadmap, the OLED MacBook Air is conspicuously absent, having been replaced by the 13.8-inch OLED machine in a separate "new" product category. The new model is expected to incorporate an LTPO+ backplane, integrated touch sensing, an under-panel camera, and a color filter integrated into the OLED encapsulation layer. 

Omdia believes it is still too early to know for sure which display manufacturer would supply panels for the device, but the firm believes that it could potentially become an important mainstream MacBook product, positioned between the LCD MacBook Air and the higher-end OLED MacBook Pro.

Meanwhile, the MacBook Air line is shown as continuing to use LCD displays right into 2030.


Of course, Apple's wholesale OLED adoption plans could change, and Omdia itself caveats that its roadmap is based on current market expectations. On that basis alone, it could be adjusted at any time according to OLED manufacturing capacity, component costs, and Apple's wider product strategy. Additionally, this is the first we've heard of a completely new MacBook line, and it's still three years out. So with all due caution, file this one under "wait and see."
